The point, I think, is that specifically designing a game to be "e-sports friendly" (cf. Starcraft II) more than often results in a game that is simply not fun to play if you don't happen to be a slightly chubby Korean who spends 16 hours a day in front of a computer (and I think even those do not find the game particularly "fun").

Starcraft I made it big because it was easy to learn but difficult to master, plus it also had a very-well written and designed single player campaign. This allowed both casual players and hardcore players to pick up the title, and at the end of the day, it presumably were the casual players who watched the big e-sports tournaments.

I don't think that the implementation of competition focused features was the problem for SC2. The bigger issue was the always-online DRM, lack of Lan functionality, and the delayed release of custom game modes.

These were big disappointments, true, but at the end of the day, what effectively killed SC II was Blizzard insisting to make it increasingly fast-paced and micro-heavy in a desperate attempt to defend their Korean esports share against the growing MOBA games. And as mentioned above, this type of gameplay simply makes the game unappealing as a game.
